title: SEBI - 0364/2004 — Dhayabhai Share & Stock Brokers Ltd. v. Securities and Exchange Board of India
text:
IN THE SECURITIES APPELLATE TRIBUNAL
MUMBAI
Appeal No. 364 of 2004
Date of decision : 13.3.2007
Dhayabhai Share & Stock Brokers Ltd. …… Appellant
Versus
Securities and Exchange Board of India
and Another …… Respondent
Mr. Vishwanath Mannadiar Advocate for the appellant.
Mr. J.J. Bhatt, Senior Advocate with Mr. U.N. Das, Advocate for the
Respondent
Coram : Justice N.K. Sodhi, Presiding Officer
R.N. Bhardwaj, Member
Per : Justice N.K. Sodhi, Presiding Officer (Oral),
The appellant before us had been working as a stock broker and was
registered with the Securities and Exchange Board of India (for short the
Board). The broking business has since been stopped. The dispute raised
herein is in regard to the fee already paid by the appellant. Every stock broker
is required to obtain a certificate of registration and one of the conditions for the
grant of that certificate is that he shall pay the amount of fees for registration in
the manner provided in the regulations. The fee that is payable is based on the
turn over of the stock broker and different rates of fee have been prescribed for
different types of transactions. It appears that at a particular point of time a
large number of stock brokers were in arrears of the registration fee payable by
them on which interest was also leviable. Given the background of the defaults,
the Board came out with a scheme called the Securities and Exchange Board of
India (Interest Liability Regularisation) Scheme, 2004 as a one time opportunity

2
to enable the stock brokers in the cash segments of stock exchanges to
regularise their defaults. Under the scheme the stock brokers who had
outstanding fee liability (principal and/or interest) as on 1st October, 2004 could
pay the entire outstanding amount of principal, if any, together with 20% of the
outstanding interest as on that date and on payment of that amount the liability
to pay the balance 80% of the outstanding interest would be wiped out. In
terms of the scheme every stock broker was required to submit the data to the
Board through the concerned stock exchange on the basis of which the fee
payable by him was worked out. It is not in dispute that the appellant submitted
the required data to the Board which contained the gross turnover of the
appellant. The data was accepted and the fee liability of the appellant was
determined.
As already observed the appellant had furnished the gross turnover data
to the Board on the basis of which its fee liability had been worked out. After
the payment had been made, the appellant furnished to the Board another data
containing the break up of its transactions and claimed refund of the amount
already paid on the plea that the jobbing transactions carried out by the
appellant carried a lower rate of fee. Since the Board had already accepted the
earlier data furnished by the appellant through the stock exchange, the
subsequent data was not accepted. It was then that the appellant filed the
present appeal against the fee liability statement furnished by the Board.
When this appeal came up for hearing on 27.6.2005, the Tribunal
observed that the parties should sit together and examine afresh the transaction
data furnished by the appellant so that its fee liability on that basis could be

3
worked out afresh. We are informed that in pursuance to the order passed by
this Tribunal, the representatives of the parties held a few meetings. Finally,
the appellant furnished to the Board through the Bombay Stock Exchange the
break up of its gross turnover showing the different nature of transactions
executed. Now that this data is available and has come through the stock
exchange, we see no reason why the Board should not examine the same and
redetermine the fee liability of the appellant. We order accordingly.
The learned senior counsel for the respondent Board points out that if
the revised data now furnished by the appellant is accepted by the Board it
would open flood gates for others whose cases have already been finalized
when the scheme was operational and that all those stock brokers may want
their fee liability to be determined afresh. We do not think that would be
possible because no one other than the appellant had pursued the matter and had
come up in appeal before this Tribunal. The learned senior counsel for the
appellant has conceded that when the Board redetermines the fee liability of
the appellant on the basis of the revised data now furnished, the appellant will
not take advantage of the scheme and will pay full interest up to the date of
payment on the amount that is found due.
The appeal stands disposed of as above with no order as to the costs.
